title: Boethius in prison
hook: condemned and waiting, he writes the Consolation of Philosophy, where Lady Philosophy comes to his cell

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's picture of love: lover, beloved, and the love between them. Your line was love in three.

A man sits in confinement, writing sad poems. Not long ago he was a powerful official at the king's court. Now, as he tells it in his own book, he's condemned, his good name gone, and he's waiting. The Muses of poetry stand around his bed, feeding him lines of grief. Then a woman appears above his head, her robe old and torn, as if rough hands had ripped pieces away. She sends the Muses packing, sits on the edge of his bed, and wipes his eyes with a fold of her dress. He knows her. She's Philosophy. This is Boethius in prison.

The book is the Consolation of Philosophy, a conversation between a broken man and the wisdom he had studied all his life. Philosophy doesn't start with comfort. She starts with diagnosis: you've forgotten who you are. Then, in the second book, comes an image: Fortune's wheel. In one passage Philosophy speaks in Fortune's own voice. I turn a wheel, Fortune says. I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unfair when it brings you down again; that's the game you agreed to play. Change isn't Fortune betraying you. Change is what Fortune is. So Philosophy asks Boethius to look at what he's lost: money, office, applause. Were they ever really his? What can be taken away was only on loan. What can't be taken is the good itself, and Philosophy leads him, step by step, toward God as that highest good, the still center the wheel turns around. Boethius was a Christian who wrote on the Trinity, yet this book never names Christ. The help comes from reason. Christian readers have still treasured it, hearing echoes of scripture. Hannah's song in First Samuel: "The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up." And Job, stripped of everything: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
screen: `WHAT CAN BE TAKEN WAS ON LOAN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that's gone badly lately, a loss, a no, a door that closed, and let it be as heavy as it is. Picture a wise friend on the edge of your bed, the way Philosophy sat with Boethius, asking what this took that was only on loan, and what's still yours; if you pray, bring both answers to God. If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Boethius in prison. A condemned man whose Consolation of Philosophy turns him from Fortune's wheel to the good that can't be taken.
Your line: the wheel turns. The still center doesn't. That's day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Christian readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss, and the image of Fortune's wheel appears in Christian art, poetry and preaching.
